subject: Banking
title: Late Payment Penalties
description: A micro-lesson that makes Late Payment Penalties usable.

hook.text: Miss a credit card payment and you get a $40 late fee plus your interest rate jumps to 29%. One mistake costs hundreds.

buildup.text: US banks collect over $14 billion annually in credit card late fees alone.

discovery.text: Penalty APRs are triggered by a single late payment. Your rate stays elevated for months, costing far more than the fee.

twist.text: The CFPB capped credit card late fees at $8 in 2024. Banks immediately sued to block the rule, protecting $14 billion.

climax.text: Late fees are designed to punish mistakes, but they generate predictable revenue banks depend on and fight to keep.

punchline.text: $14 billion in late fees. Banks sued to keep charging them.

quiz.question: What happens to your interest rate after a missed credit card payment?
options: It can jump to a penalty rate of 29% or higher

details.summary: Late payment penalties on credit cards, mortgages, and loans generate billions in annual revenue for banks. These fees are designed to be punitive enough to incentivize on-time payment but are often disproportionate to the actual cost banks incur.
details.whyItMatters: Late fees hit people hardest when they can least afford them, often compounding financial distress. Understanding that these fees are profit centers rather than cost recovery reveals the economics behind bank penalty structures.
takeaways: Credit card late fees have been as high as $39 per occurrence
The CFPB proposed capping credit card late fees at $8 in 2024
Banks earn over $12 billion annually from credit card late fees alone

faq.question: How much do banks actually earn from late fees?
faq.answer: Banks earned over $12 billion from credit card late fees in a recent year. The actual cost to the bank of processing a late payment is estimated at around $3, meaning the vast majority of the $30-39 fee is pure profit.

faq.question: Will late fee caps reduce bank revenue significantly?
faq.answer: If the CFPB's $8 cap takes effect, banks estimate they would lose $9 billion annually. Banks have argued they would offset this by increasing interest rates and reducing rewards programs, passing the cost back to consumers in other ways.
